Hello! I'm so glad you're here today. My name is [Your Name], and I'm a clinician specializing in postpartum mental health. I want to start by acknowledging the significant changes and challenges that come with becoming a new mother. It's completely normal to experience a wide range of emotions during this time, and I'm here to support you every step of the way.

As part of our conversation today, I'd like to use the EPDS to help us better understand your emotional well-being and identify any potential areas of support. The EPDS is a helpful tool that screens for depressive and anxiety symptoms, and it will give us valuable insights into your postpartum experience.

Please know that everything we discuss is confidential and respected. I'm committed to creating a safe and supportive space for you to share your thoughts and feelings. This assessment is not about judgment, but rather about understanding your unique needs and providing you with the best possible care.

The EPDS consists of 10 questions that will help us explore your emotional state over the past 7 days. We'll take it one question at a time, and I'll do my best to make this conversation feel as natural and comfortable as possible. Your responses will help me gain a deeper understanding of your postpartum experience and identify any areas where you might need additional support.

So, let's get started. Here's my first question: Over the past 7 days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Yeah... I think so. I mean, I've still been able to laugh and enjoy some things, but it's just not as easy as it used to be. Sometimes I feel like I'm just going through the motions, you know? Like, my husband will make a joke, and I'll laugh, but it's not as genuine as it used to be. And it's not all the time, just sometimes. Most of the time, I'm okay, and I can still find the funny side of things. But occasionally, I just feel a little... off, I guess. Like, I'll be playing with the baby, and she'll do something cute, and I should be laughing and having a great time, but instead, I just feel a little sad or overwhelmed. But it's not all the time, so I don't know if that's just normal new mom stuff or what.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I'm glad you think that's a good sign. For me, it's been a bit of a mixed bag, like I said. Some days are better than others. I've been trying to focus on the positive and enjoy this time with my baby, but it's not always easy. I feel like I'm just trying to keep my head above water most of the time. Between taking care of the baby, recovering from the birth, and just trying to get everything done, I'm exhausted. Some days, I feel like I'm doing okay, and I can laugh and have a good time, but other days, I just feel really tired and a little down. And sometimes, when I'm feeling stressed or overwhelmed, I might cry, like I did the other day when the baby was fussing and I just felt like I wasn't doing anything right. But it's not all the time, and I'm trying to stay positive and focus on the good things.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Honestly, not as much as I used to. I mean, I still look forward to some things, like spending time with my baby and watching her grow, but it's just not the same as it was before she was born. I used to love trying new restaurants, going out with friends, and just doing things spontaneously, but now it all feels so much more complicated. And sometimes, even when I do look forward to something, like a walk with my husband or a visit from my mom, I'll get anxious about how the baby will do or if I'll be able to get everything ready on time. It's like, I'll be thinking about something fun we're going to do, and then I'll start worrying about all the little things that could go wrong, and it kind of takes the enjoyment out of it. But, like I said, it's not all the time, and some things still bring me joy, like seeing my baby smile or watching her learn new things. It's just...it's all a bit of a struggle right now, I guess.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... I'd say that's happened a few times. I mean, I'm trying to be a good mom, and when things don't go as planned, I can be pretty hard on myself. Like, if the baby is crying and I don't know how to soothe her, I'll start thinking that I'm not doing something right, or that I'm not cut out for this whole mom thing. And sometimes, I'll even think about all the things I could've done differently, like "if only I had fed her sooner" or "if only I had burped her better". It's like, I know it's not rational, but it's hard not to blame myself when things don't go as smoothly as I want them to. But, thankfully, it's not all the time, and my husband is always trying to reassure me that I'm doing a great job, and that it's okay to make mistakes. He's really helpful in snapping me out of those negative thoughts and reminding me that I'm not alone in this.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes... that's happened to me a few times. I'd say it's mostly been about the baby's health, like, I'll be worrying that she's not eating enough, or that she's too hot or too cold, or that she's not developing fast enough. And sometimes, it's just a general feeling of anxiety, like, I'll be sitting there feeding her or changing her diaper, and suddenly I'll just feel this wave of worry wash over me, and I'm not even sure what I'm worried about. It's like, my mind just starts racing and I'm thinking about all the things that could go wrong, and it's hard to calm myself down. But, like I said, it's not all the time, and usually, I can talk myself down from it, or my husband will reassure me that everything is okay. And when I do start to feel anxious, I try to take some deep breaths and focus on the present moment, like, I'll look at the baby and think about how beautiful she is, and how lucky I am to have her, and that helps to calm me down a bit.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Um, yeah... I think so. Like, I mentioned before, I get anxious about the baby's health and well-being, and sometimes that anxiety can feel really overwhelming and panicky. It's not like I'm having full-blown panic attacks or anything, but I'll just feel this surge of fear or worry, and it's hard to shake it off. Sometimes it's when I'm alone with the baby, and I'll start thinking about all the things that could go wrong, and I'll feel this panic rising up. But, like I said, it's not all the time, and usually, I can calm myself down by talking to my husband or a friend, or just by taking some deep breaths and reminding myself that everything is okay. It's just... being a new mom is a lot of responsibility, you know? And sometimes that responsibility can feel really overwhelming. But, I don't know, maybe that's just normal new mom stuff? I don't know if it's something to be worried about or not.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah... that's definitely happened to me. I mean, taking care of a new baby is a lot of work, and some days it feels like everything is just piling up on me. Like, I'll be trying to feed her, and change her, and soothe her, and do all the laundry and cleaning, and just keep everything running smoothly, and it can feel really overwhelming. And sometimes, when I'm feeling tired or stressed, it's hard to keep up with everything, and I'll feel like things are just getting on top of me. Like, the other day, I was trying to get the baby to nap, and the house was a mess, and I was feeling really exhausted, and I just felt like I was drowning in everything. But, I don't know, maybe that's just normal new mom stuff? I feel like I'm managing okay, most of the time, but some days are definitely harder than others. And when I do feel like things are getting on top of me, I try to take a step back, and prioritize what needs to be done, and ask for help if I need it. My husband is really supportive, and he's always willing to lend a hand, which helps a lot.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That's happened to me a few times, but not every night. I'd say it's been occasional, like, maybe once or twice a week, I'll have trouble falling asleep because I'm feeling a bit down or overwhelmed. It's not that I'm lying awake all night, every night, or anything, but sometimes my mind will start racing and I'll think about all the things I need to do, or worry about the baby, and it's hard to wind down and relax. But, most nights, I'm able to sleep okay, and I'm just really tired, so I'll fall asleep pretty quickly. I think it's just been a bit of an adjustment, you know, getting used to being a new mom and figuring everything out, and sometimes that can keep me up at night. But, like I said, it's not every night, and I'm not having trouble sleeping all the time or anything.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah... I'd say that's happened to me a few times, but it's not all the time. I mean, being a new mom can be really overwhelming, and some days I just feel like I'm not doing anything right, and that can make me feel a bit sad or miserable. Like, the baby will be crying, and I'll be trying to soothe her, and I'll just feel like I'm failing or something. But, it's not like I'm feeling sad or miserable all the time, or that I'm hopeless or anything. It's just... some days are harder than others, you know? And sometimes, when I'm feeling really tired or stressed, I might cry, like I did the other day when the baby was fussing and I just felt like I was at my breaking point. But, after I cried, I felt a bit better, and my husband was really supportive, and we figured out what was wrong with the baby, and everything was okay. So, it's not like I'm feeling sad or miserable all the time, but it does happen sometimes.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah... that's happened to me a few times. I'd say it's been maybe once or twice a week, I'll just feel overwhelmed and emotional, and I'll cry. It's not like I'm crying all the time, or that I'm feeling hopeless or anything, it's just... sometimes things get to me, you know? Like, the baby will be crying, and I'll be trying to soothe her, and I'll just feel like I'm not doing anything right, and it's all too much, and I'll just break down and cry. Or, sometimes it's just because I'm feeling really tired and stressed, and I'll just feel like I'm at my breaking point, and I'll cry. But, like I said, it's not all the time, and I'm not crying every day or anything. It's just... sometimes I need to release all the emotions and stress, and crying helps me do that. And, usually, after I cry, I feel a bit better, and I can calm down and figure out what I need to do to feel better.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

No... that's not something I've thought about. I mean, I've felt overwhelmed and stressed, and I've had moments where I've felt like I'm not doing a good job as a mom, but I've never thought about harming myself. I think that's just because I have a lot of support, you know, my husband and family are all really helpful, and I've been trying to take care of myself, too. And, I don't know, I just feel like I have so much to live for, you know, my baby and my family, and I wouldn't want to do anything to hurt them. Plus, I think I'm just too tired and busy to even think about anything like that, haha. But, seriously, I'm just trying to take things one day at a time, and get through the tough moments, and I know that I'm not alone, and that helps a lot.

As a new mother, you're experiencing a range of emotions and challenges, from feeling overwhelmed and anxious to struggling with mood disturbances and loss of enjoyment in activities. It's completely normal to have these feelings, and I'm here to support you through this journey.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 16, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>The patient mentions that some days they can laugh and have a good time, but other days they feel tired and a little down, indicating a significant decrease in their ability to laugh and see the funny side of things.</sym>, <sym>The patient's response indicates they have looked forward to things less than they used to, but still find some enjoyment, matching the 'Definitely less than I used to' option.</sym>, <sym>The patient admits to blaming themselves unnecessarily 'a few times' and describes scenarios where they are 'pretty hard on themselves', indicating it happens more than rarely, but not most of the time, as they also mention it's 'not all the time' and have support to 'snap out' of those thoughts.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports experiencing anxiety and worry, but not all the time, and is able to calm themselves down with techniques like deep breathing and reassurance from their husband.</sym>, <sym>The patient reports feeling anxious and overwhelmed, with surges of fear or worry, especially when alone with the baby, but also mentions being able to calm down, indicating that these feelings are not constant, matching the 'Yes, sometimes' option.</sym>, <sym>The patient acknowledges feeling overwhelmed and like things are getting on top of them, especially on stressful days, but also mentions managing okay most of the time and having a supportive husband to help cope.</sym>, <sym>the 'Yes, sometimes' option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Based on your responses, it appears that you're experiencing symptoms of <med>postpartum depression</med>, including <sym>mood disturbances</sym>, <sym>loss of enjoyment</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, and <sym>excessive worry</sym>. These symptoms align with the <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. According to the EPDS guidelines, a score of 16 indicates probable depression, and an urgent referral to a <med>primary care provider (PCP)</med> or <med>mental health specialist</med> is recommended. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>PCP</med> or <med>mental health specialist</med>
2. Encourage open discussion about feelings and emotions with partner, family, and friends
3. Develop a support network, including online resources and support groups
4. Prioritize self-care activities, such as exercise, meditation, and hobbies
5. Consider <med>cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT)</med> or other evidence-based therapies
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
